**Phishing Awareness Session – 20-Minute Plan for Architecture Firm in Winterthur**

---

### 1. Why This Matters (1 min)

• **Your data is the firm’s crown jewels**: client blueprints, copyrighted drawings, fee schedules, project proposals.  
• **One successful phish can shut down a project**, expose sensitive info, or trigger a costly data‑breach cleanup.  
• The “parcel-delivery” story isn’t isolated – scammers learn from headlines (new building permits, COVID‑related supply chain emails, Swiss‑specific tax changes).  

---

### 2. The “How” – What Is Phishing? (3 min)

| Step | Typical Technique | Goal |
|------|-------------------|------|
| **1. Harvest Credentials** | Fake login page that looks identical to Google, Office 365, or your firm’s own intranet | Steal usernames/passwords |
| **2. Social Engineering** | Crafted message (email, SMS, Teams message, even a phone call) that triggers an emotional reaction (urgency, fear, curiosity, reward) | Get you to click, open attachment, or type password |
| **3. Delivery** | Email spoofing (fake “From” address), redirect through malicious link, or a convincing look‑alike site | Direct to the fake page |
| **4. Exploitation** | Stolen credentials sold or used immediately to access corporate emails, cloud storage (SharePoint/OneDrive), CAD files, financial systems | Access to proprietary designs or sabotage projects |
| **5. Hide tracks** | Phishers use burner email, VPN proxies, temporary servers; logs are wiped quickly | Deny attribution |

*Key concept*: **Phishing = Social engineering + malicious link or attachment.**

---

### 3. Real‑World Template of a “Parcel-Delivery” Phish (5 min)

Below are exact wording examples that **have actually appeared** to Swiss companies:

#### a) Email from a “Swiss Post” Spoof

```
Subject: Ihre Paketlieferung – bitte unterschreiben [Link]

Dear [Name]

Swiss Post could not deliver your parcel today due to insufficient signature. To avoid additional fees and storage costs, please click the link below and sign electronically within the next 24 hours.

[Link: https://secure-swisspost-login.ch/verify-signature]

Note: Your login credentials are required on the next page to confirm identity.

Best regards
Swiss Post – Delivery Services
```

*What looks real*  
• Official‑style language, familiar logo (but low‑resolution or slightly different).  
• Sense of urgency (“24 hours”).  
*Red flags*  
• Unexpected sender address (e.g., `postdelivery@swiss‑delivery.com` instead of `post.ch`).  
• Link domain doesn’t look like “swisspost.ch”.  
• Request for login credentials *in a message you didn’t initiate*.

#### b) Microsoft‑style “Password Expiry” Phish

```
From: Outlook Support <security-notifications@outlook.com>
To: All Employees <team@firmname.ch>
Subject: Important: Your Outlook password will expire in 12 hours – renew now

Dear Colleagues,

In accordance with firmwide security policies, your Outlook password will expire within the next 12 hours. Please follow this secure link to update it:

[https://login-microsoft.com/reauth/firmname]

Failure to comply may result in loss of email access and project calendar privileges.  
No further email reminder will be sent.

Microsoft IT Support
```

*What looks real*  
• Uses the real Outlook logo, correct company name.  
• Threat of loss of access is plausible.  
*Red flags*  
• Sender domain ends with `.com` even though your firm uses Office 365 through a `.ch` tenant.  
• The link path does not start with `https://login.microsoftonline.com/` but looks slightly mangled.  
• Request to “renew now” without a prior security notice.

#### c) “CEO” or “Office Manager” Impersonation

```
From: marco.looser@firmaarchitektur.ch (office.manager)
To: Everyone <team@firmaarchitektur.ch>
Subject: Urgent – Need You to Transfer Funds for a Supplier

Hi All,

I’m on a call with the supplier for the XYZ condo project and they need immediate payment. Please log into our bank portal at:

[https://firmbank.swiss/login]

Enter the credentials from the shared spreadsheet in OneDrive. Let me know once you’ve completed the transfer, thanks!

Marco

```

*What looks real*  
• Uses your own colleague’s name and email.  
• References a real project (XYZ condo).  
*Red flags*  
• Requests you provide login credentials (never normal).  
• Asks you to use a link that isn’t your bank’s official URL (often a look‑alike with a slight misspelling like `firmbank.swiz`).

#### d) “Zoom / Teams Meeting Invitation” Phish

```
From: IT-Support <it-support@firmaarchitektur.ch>
To: All Employees <team@firmaarchitektur.ch>
Subject: Reminder: Weekly Project Sync – click here to join

Please click the link below to join the usual Thursday project sync. The link is only valid for today:

https://zoom.us/j/123456789?pwd=xxxx

If the link does not open in your browser, double-click the attached .ics file.

IT Department
```

*What looks real*  
• Appears to be from IT, mentions a regular meeting.  
*Red flags*  
• URL contains random numbers and may differ from the real Zoom join link you usually see in Teams/Outlook invites.  
• Attached `.ics` or `.zip` could contain an exploit if opened blindly.  
• Even if the meeting exists, verify via official calendar invite before clicking anything.

---

### 4. How to Recognise a Phish – Quick Checklist (4 min)

| Red Flag | Action |
|----------|--------|
| **Unexpected email / message** from a sender you don’t usually exchange sensitive info with, or a known sender whose behavior is atypical | **Pause → Verify** |
| **Urgency language** (“Act now”, “Immediate”, “Will expire in X hours”) | **Slow down – treat as emergency, not a race** |
| **Generic greetings** (“Dear user”, “Valued customer”) instead of your name | **Suspicious – verify** |
| **Misspellings, awkward grammar** (“Login your account”, “Your password has been expired”) | **Flag** |
| **Links that don’t match known domains** (hover mouse over link; see the real URL before clicking) | **Do NOT click** |
| **Requests for credentials, credit‑card, or sensitive data via email** | **NEVER reply or fill out anything** |
| **Attachments you weren’t expecting** (especially `.exe`, `.scr`, `.zip`, `.js`, `.docm` without a prior request) | **Do not open** – ask sender via a secondary channel (phone, Slack direct message) |
| **Sense of reward/punishment**: “Congrats! You won a prize”, “Account locked – pay now” | **Double‑check** |
| **Domain mismatch**: `[fake]` instead of `[official]` (e.g., `outlook-secure.com` vs `outlook.com`) | **Report** |

*Quick tip*: **Hover over any link before clicking**. Most email clients show the real destination.  
If it looks off, **copy the link address, paste into a plaintext note, and run a WHOIS/URL‑check via VirusTotal or simply call the person back**.

---

### 5. What to Do – Your Two‑Second Decision Flow (2 min)

1. **Pause** – Do not click or type anything while reading the message.
2. **Verify source** –  
   • Does the email come from the exact address you expect?  
   • Is the tone consistent with the real sender?  
   • Does the URL resolve to the official domain (e.g., `https://login.firmaarchitektur.ch`)?  
3. **Use a second channel** –  
   • Send a DM on Teams or call the person directly and ask, “Did you send me that link?”
4. **Report if unsure** –  
   • Forward the suspicious message to IT/Security (or designate a “phish test” inbox e.g., `phish@firmaarchitektur.ch`).  
   • Mark it in Outlook/Outlook on the web as **phishing** (many tools auto‑report).
5. **Delete / ignore** – If confirmed malicious, delete immediately; don’t even read the contents.

*Example script*:  
> “Hi Lisa, I just got an email that looks like it’s from Swiss Post about my parcel. The link seems off – did you send it to me? In the meantime I’ll delete it and maybe forward it to IT just to be safe.”  

That short interaction stops the attack cold.

---

### 6. Reinforcement Methods (2 min)

• **Post‑session quiz** (2‑3 quick questions over Teams chat: “Which of the following is a red flag – urgent language?”).  
• **Share physical cheat sheet**: a one‑page PDF with the checklist and example phish snippets you can laminate and stick on keyboards or near printers.  
• **Monthly “Phish of the Month”** – send out a real-world scam that circulated locally (maybe a fake tax form from Swiss Federal Taxation Office) so people stay alert.  
• **Automated tools** you can request from IT:  
  – **Training via KnowBe4 or similar** (interactive phishing simulations with low‑risk click‑through).  
  – **Spam/Phish gateway** that inspects incoming mail and rewrites suspiciously mismatched domains.

---

### 7. Takeaway Message (1 min)

> **“When something screams ‘urgent’, verify before you react.”**  
> Treat any request for login, money, or private info that comes via a link or attachment as *automatic* suspicion. One extra minute to double‑check could prevent a stolen design file, a project delay, or an invoice fraud that takes weeks to untangle.

---

### Quick Slides (you can project or hand out)

| Slide Title | Content |
|-------------|---------|
| **Slide 0** | Welcome – why this matters for a 25‑person architecture firm |
| **Slide 1** | How phishing works (four‑step diagram) |
| **Slide 2** | Real example – fake “Swiss Post parcel” email |
| **Slide 3** | Real example – fake “Outlook password expiry” email |
| **Slide 4** | Real example – “CEO asks for bank transfer” spoof |
| **Slide 5** | Quick spot‑that‑phish checklist (visual bullets) |
| **Slide 6** | Two‑second follow‑up actions (pause, verify, secondary channel, report) |
| **Slide 7** | Office resources – where to forward & what simulations to expect |
| **Slide 8** | Final line – “Stop, Look, Verify, Report.” |

---

### 8. Q&A (remaining time)

Encourage participation: “Has anyone ever received something that looked odd but wasn’t sure what to do?” Share the answer using the checklist.

---

**Bottom line:** Keep the session *action‑oriented*, show *real* messages that could arrive in Winterthur offices (Swiss Post, Microsoft, Zoom, internal IT), and drill the “Pause → Verify → Report” reflex. In a 20‑minute slot you’ll leave the team with concrete steps and vivid mental models, dramatically reducing the chance the next “parcel delivery” story ends with a data breach. Good luck—your vigilance directly protects blueprints, client trust, and the firm’s reputation.
